opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think my view has shifted a fair amount over the last few years.

Early on, a lot of us in the field had a bit of a skeptical attitude toward toy experiments. The worry was that you train a little transformer on some synthetic grammar or some arithmetic task, you find a nice clean mechanism, and then it's not at all clear that anything you learned transfers to the giant model trained on the whole internet. The behaviors we actually care about in big language models seemed to depend on scale and on the messiness of natural data, so it felt like the toy setting might be throwing away exactly the thing you wanted to study.

I've come around to thinking that's too pessimistic, for a couple of reasons. One is that some of the phenomena we see in large models turn out to have surprisingly faithful analogues in small settings. Things like in-context learning: you can set up a synthetic task where a model has to infer, say, a linear function or a simple automaton from examples in its context, and you see behavior that looks qualitatively similar to what happens at scale. And in that setting you can actually ask precise questions. What algorithm is the model implementing? Is it doing something like gradient descent, or Bayesian inference, or something else? You can compare against known optimal learners, which you just can't do when the "task" is all of the internet.

The second reason is that synthetic data gives you control over the data distribution, and a lot of the interesting questions about language models are really questions about how properties of the training data turn into properties of the model. If you want to know whether a model can build a coherent representation of some underlying world state, or whether it learns to distinguish between true and false statements, or how it handles conflicting sources, you can design data where you know the ground truth and you can vary exactly one thing at a time. That kind of causal experiment is basically impossible with real pretraining corpora.

That said, I don't think toy experiments are self-justifying. The way I'd put it now is that they're most valuable as part of a loop. You observe something puzzling in a real model, you build a minimal synthetic setting that reproduces it, you figure out the mechanism there, and then, crucially, you go back to the real model and check whether the prediction holds. When that loop closes, you've learned something real. When people stop at the toy stage and just assume it transfers, that's where things go wrong.

So I guess the short version is: I used to think of toy experiments as a sort of warm-up or a sanity check, and now I think of them as one of the main tools we have for making precise scientific claims about these systems, as long as we stay honest about validating them against the real thing.

r002.rationale: It says phenomena in large models can have faithful analogues in small settings and that toy mechanisms can yield real insights when validated against the real model.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Lee et al., a beaker manipulation task, or representations from human-written versus synthetic instructions.

r005.rationale: It cautions against assuming toy results transfer, but does not address the named paper, hidden representations, or whether simple experiments establish what larger models encode.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my view has actually gone through a couple of phases on this. When I started working on things like compositional generalization, back in the SCAN days, I was pretty optimistic that if you could build a small, controlled environment where you knew exactly what the right generalization was, you'd learn something that transferred directly to the big models. And for a while I think the field, myself included, got a little burned by that. We'd find some failure mode in a toy setting, write the paper about how neural networks fundamentally can't do X, and then two years later a model trained on enough data just quietly does X.

So there was a period where I was fairly skeptical of toy experiments as a way of making claims about what models can or can't learn. The thing I've come around to is that they're really bad for making capability claims and really good for making mechanistic claims. If I want to know whether a language model can represent the state of a board game, or whether in-context learning is implementing something like gradient descent, or whether a model builds an internal model of the world it's describing, a synthetic setting is enormously useful because I can actually define what the ground truth is. In natural language I don't have access to the true semantics, I don't have a clean notion of what the world state is, and so I can't ask whether the model has recovered it.

So the Othello work, the work on tracking entity states in synthetic text, those are places where I think the synthetic setup isn't a stand-in for the real thing, it's the only place the question is well posed. And then the real test is whether the probing techniques or the interpretability tools you develop there actually say something when you point them at a large pretrained model. Sometimes they do, sometimes they don't, and the gap is itself informative.

The other shift is in what I think a toy experiment is for in the first place. Early on, the implicit goal was usually to show a limitation. Now I think of them more as a way of generating hypotheses about what a training process is likely to produce. If I can show that a small transformer, trained on data with a certain structure, reliably develops a certain kind of internal representation, that gives me a specific thing to go look for at scale, rather than a general claim about transformers. That's a more modest role, but I think it's the one where the experiments have actually held up.

r001.rationale: The response says toy experiments are poor for broad capability claims, but it does not state that strong performance on a toy dataset need not imply real-world usefulness.

r002.rationale: It says probing techniques and interpretability tools developed in synthetic settings sometimes “do” say something when applied to large pretrained models.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Lee et al., a beaker manipulation task, or a comparison between human-written and synthetic instructions.

r004.rationale: The response does not report intervention results or compare effects across natural-data and synthetic-data versions of the beaker task.

r005.rationale: The response favors using toy experiments to generate hypotheses rather than broad claims, but does not state that the experiments in “Language Models as Agent Models” cannot establish what larger models encode in their hidden representations.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more interested in them, but also more careful about what conclusions to draw from them. There are really two different questions: can we construct a setting where a model exhibits some behavior, and is that setting actually a good explanation of what’s happening in a large language model trained on natural text? A synthetic experiment can give you a very clean answer to the first question without necessarily answering the second.

The appeal is that you can control things that are almost impossible to control in a natural corpus. You know exactly what information was available during training. You can change one property of the data and see whether the behavior changes. That makes it possible to distinguish explanations that would otherwise look identical.

But the connection back to the real system is essential. If you think you’ve isolated a mechanism in a toy setting, what does that mechanism predict about a model trained on natural language? Can you intervene on that model and get the effect you expect? I’m most excited about work that goes back and forth between those settings, where the synthetic experiment helps formulate a hypothesis and the larger experiment tells you whether you’ve captured something that matters.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes demonstrating a behavior in a synthetic setting from explaining behavior in a large language model, but it does not discuss structured-model performance or real-world usefulness.

r002.rationale: It proposes testing synthetic hypotheses on larger models, but does not state that interpretability findings from toy experiments can generalize to large-scale language models.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention the Lee et al. study, beaker manipulation, or its instruction conditions.

r004.rationale: The response does not report intervention effects in natural-data and synthetic-data versions of the beaker study.

r005.rationale: It says synthetic experiments alone may not explain behavior in large language models, but does not address hidden representations or the claim about correspondingly more complex encoding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more cautious about what we can conclude from them, while still finding them incredibly useful. In a toy setting, you can control what information is available to the model and isolate a particular hypothesis. That’s much harder when you’re looking at a language model trained on a huge corpus whose contents you don’t fully understand.

But there’s a gap between showing that a model can learn some behavior in a synthetic setting and showing that this explains what’s happening in a large language model. The training distribution matters, the scale matters, and there may be several different ways to solve the same task.

So I increasingly think of these experiments as a way to develop hypotheses and test whether a proposed mechanism is possible. Then you need to go back to the larger, messier setting and ask whether the predictions actually hold. The strongest work, to me, moves back and forth between those two settings.
